items.title: Apple employee AI budgets cut to reduce costs
items.content_html:
Employees relying on third-party AI use to perform work at Apple will need to cut back as funding has been reduced by as much as a third for some.

Internal artificial intelligence use has become too expensive for many companies, including Apple, as returns for the expenses continue to wane. Apple uses the features for coding assistance, bug hunting, and more, but reliance on these expensive tools is proving costly.

According to a report from Bloomberg, Apple has already cut available funds from $300 to $200 per engineer. Some cuts have even seen cuts down to $100, and yet some still have as little as $25 in AI funding for their projects.

Apple allegedly allows employees to request higher allowances on a per-use basis. The move appears to reflect a pulling back the rest of the tech industry has seen as the experimental phase of AI ends.

No signs of doom

The report seems to suggest there is confusion for the move while hanging the threat of potential layoffs over the whole thing. However, it also says that many engineers reported Apple employees not coming close to the already generous $300 limit.

While some might suspect this cost-cutting is some kind of threat, it is more likely a bureaucratic one. If employees aren't spending what is allotted, then freeing up those funds for other projects makes more sense.

The reality of artificial intelligence has been slow to set in on the wider investors and "lunatic fringe." It is a capable technology that can accelerate workflows and find bugs at a scale no human could, but it is also limited in its usefulness among experts in their craft.

Developers aren't vibe coding the next update to Pages or Notes.

Apple is also working to develop more functional AI systems that run on its own Apple Foundation Models. There's also the fact that Apple's Mac lineup are incredibly capable of running some models locally, thus minimizing the need for additional paid tokens.

As the AI boom turns more into an AI trickle and the investment bubble pops, budgeting around the new reality of the technology is only logical.

items.title: macOS 27.3 brings Live Activities to all supported Macs
items.content_html:
Dynamic Island may be exclusive to the PROLED MacBook Pro, but Live Activities are coming to all Macs capable of running macOS 27.3.

Live Activities, previously exclusive to the iPhone and iPad, let you keep track of timers, orders, and whether you're using screen recording. This is all done through a little bubble that pops up at the top of the screen.

With the PROLED MacBook Pro, announced on October 28, Apple brought Live Activities over to the Mac. "With Live Activities, users can now get timely updates at a glance, and can accept an AirDrop request or pause a song with a tap of their finger," said Apple in the accompanying press release.

However, Live Activities won't be exclusive to the new laptop. The first beta of macOS 27.3, released on Tuesday, revealed that all supported Macs will get this feature.

Live Activities are available at the top of the screen.

In short, all Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 27.3 or later will gain access to Dynamic Island. This includes MacBooks with a notch at the top, and older laptops like the M1 MacBook Pro and MacBook Air.

macOS 27.3 offers Live Activities related to built-in applications, including Apple Music, Clock, and Voice Memos, among others. Developers will have the option to implement Live Activities for third-party applications as well.

Live Activities as a feature, meanwhile, debuted on iPhone as part of the iOS 16.1 update in 2022. iPadOS 17 later expanded the feature to the iPad Platform the following year.

items.title: StandBy on iPhone Duo is even better than you thought
items.content_html:
StandBy is a feature that has been available on iPhones since 2023, but with iPhone Duo, Apple has upgraded it to become a whole new way to access glanceable information not just when charging, but whenever it's not being used.

Since StandBy was added to the iOS 17 feature list at WWDC in June of 2023, it's been limited in a couple of key ways. The iPhone Duo addresses both.

The first limitation is that StandBy only works when an iPhone is being charged, whether plugged into a cable or attached to a MagSafe charger. The other is that iPhones have relatively small displays, so there's only so much room for information.

But the iPhone Duo doesn't need to be charging, and its large 7.6-inch display has plenty of space to spare. That means it's the perfect device for StandBy.

Here, we're going to get into what StandBy is, how it works on the iPhone Duo, and why you should give it a try. Then we'll dive into some of the apps whose StandBy widgets you should check out.

StandBy, a desk and bedtime display

StandBy is a feature that takes an otherwise dormant iPhone and turns it into a smart display of sorts. It can display the time, the date, and all kinds of other information that's just waiting to be glanced at rather than interacted with.

That's why StandBy is especially useful on a desk while you work, or on a table while you sleep. Whether it's your calendar at the office or a big-screen clock and your alarm overnight, StandBy can display some incredibly helpful information.

At night, when the iPhone's light sensor detects it's dark, StandBy enables a low-light Night Mode. Everything turns red to not disrupt your sleep, but the same information remains available. You can finally ditch that old alarm clock.

StandBy can also be used to turn an unused iPhone into a digital photo frame of sorts. And while widgets are glanceable, you can still tap them to interact with them or open their app.

But that's how StandBy works on any compatible iPhone. Things get much more interesting with an iPhone Duo.

StandBy but better

With no need for the iPhone Duo to be charging, StandBy is much easier to take advantage of. And that's good news, because you'll want to use it much more than you did with your old iPhone.

While StandBy can still be used when the iPhone Duo is closed, it can also be activated in two new ways. Place the iPhone Duo into tent mode, and its outer display lights up in StandBy mode automatically.

Similarly, open the iPhone Duo and stand it up, and a new, much larger StandBy mode reveals itself. This works whether you're using a case with a kickstand or the iPhone Duo's book mode to prop it up.

There are options to govern how all of this works, and you can disable the whole StandBy feature, or just tent mode and upright mode independently. You can also require the iPhone Duo to be charging and control if and when the display turns itself off, great for when it isn't charging at the time.

As you might expect, you'll get a different StandBy view and different options depending on which display is being used.

Tent mode

In tent mode, the iPhone Duo uses its outer display for StandBy. It offers a range of styles, colors, and content in what Apple calls "faces," much like Apple Watch and HomeView faces. Think of them as saved views.

Swiping left or right cycles through the available faces. For faces with widgets, swiping up and down on a widget cycles through all of those that have been configured for that face.

By default, there are a handful of faces preconfigured right out of the box:

  • Analog clock: A clock with customizable colors and complications
  • Digital clock: A digital clock, again with customizable colors and complications
  • Photos: A curated photo collection with options for albums, pets, and more.
  • Weather: A weather face that can be customized to show different information and locations.
  • Calendar: A full-screen calendar view with the date and time.
  • Modular: Similar to the Apple Watch face of the same name, this face can be customized to show different app widgets.

You can also add new faces based on those preinstalled options. This allows you to have different Modular faces with different widgets, for example.

Tent mode is great, and it's generally how you'll use StandBy overnight. But the inner display is where StandBy shines.

Book mode

StandBy makes full use of the inner display when the iPhone Duo is vertical. It can be stood up in book mode or opened flat while using a kickstand; both will work.

The inner display is split down the middle, providing two columns that can be configured individually. But there are no preset faces like Calendar and Weather, so swiping left and right does nothing.

Instead, you're given free rein over how to set up your StandBy view, adding widgets as you please. But there's one thing to consider that can be considered either a limitation or a feature.

In book mode, the left side of the display has space for two small widgets at the top and one larger widget at the bottom. The right side houses one single large widget that fills that side of the display. This layout cannot be changed.

That doesn't mean that there aren't still plenty of ways to make book mode StandBy look great, because there are. And there is no shortage of options when it comes to choosing the right widget for your StandBy face.

Apps and their widgets

Like StandBy on other iPhones, the iPhone Duo has an array of Apple-designed widgets for you to choose from. They range from calendar views to world clocks to photo frames and many other in-between.

But StandBy also surfaces widgets from your installed apps, much like those that can be placed on the iPhone's home screen. It's here, paired with book mode, that the true customizability of StandBy on iPhone Duo can be found.

The larger display afforded by book mode means you have space for more widgets of varying sizes. And remember, you can also stack widgets on top of one another with a vertical swipe cycling through that stack.

How you configure your favorite StandBy setup will depend on you and your needs. It's no good having a big, interactive calendar beside your bed while you sleep, for example.

But if you're looking for a way to display useful, glanceable data, there are some great options that hook into the third-party apps you use every day. We're going to highlight just a few here, but be sure to check your own favorite apps for StandBy widgets, too.

  • Fantastical: Its large calendar view is brilliant as a half-screen widget on the right side of the iPhone Duo.
  • CARROT Weather: The iPhone Duo has a built-in weather app, but this one adds high-information widgets, including live radar maps.
  • Timery: Great, quick access to time tracking options, including starting new timers.
  • Things: Visibility and instant checking off of all of your most important tasks.
  • Overcast: See the artwork for the currently playing podcast as well as playback controls.
  • Reddit: See popular photos from across Reddit, including cat pics.
  • Batteries: It's a built-in widget, but a glanceable view of your devices' batteries is so great that it still deserves to be on this list.

Using your iPhone even when you aren't

Many of us are trying to use our iPhones less, but that doesn't mean that it can't still be useful. StandBy turns an idle iPhone into something a way to see useful information without ever having to touch it.

With iPhone Duo, StandBy is a whole different beast. Sure, some of its new features are coming to other iPhones with iOS 27.3, but it still has a huge advantage.

The iPhone Duo's big inner display makes it a great smart display, with greater data density than any other iPhone. And that alone makes it the perfect StandBy device.

items.title: Apple TV 'Silo' might get a spinoff
items.content_html:
Citing sources familiar with the matter, Sigmund Judge claims that Apple TV is commissioning a "Silo" sequel. Judge, who has been right about things like this in the past, says that there are still some standing sets, and hires for the project have begun. Obviously, there's no premiere date, given that production hasn't started.

Exclusive: Silo's fourth and final season will be succeeded by an expansion/spinoff at Apple TV.

items.title: Apple is reportedly doubling orders for a new MacBook Neo
items.content_html:
The MacBook Neo was a massive success. If component suppliers can be believed, Apple expects the second-gen model to do twice as well.

Apple is currently forecast to introduce the second-generation MacBook Neo in the first half of 2027, with some performance updates. When it does ship, Apple is seemingly betting the new model will be a much bigger seller than the first version.

According to DigiTimes, supply chain sources say they were given a shipment forecast from Apple for the MacBook Neo. The forecast is for 16 million units in 2027, double the 8 million units of the current 2026 run.

The comparison isn't quite a doubling of shipments if you use comparative timeframes. The MacBook Neo was announced and released in early March, meaning the 2026 shipments for the model cover ten months, not the twelve of a full year.

Expected continued success

The launch of the MacBook Neo was stratospheric for Apple, with then-CEO Tim Cook saying it was the "best launch week ever for first-time Mac customers."

It was so successful that Apple doubled production to keep up with demand. Suppliers were forced to race to catch up with Apple's increased order for the model in May.

The model was also credited with helping Apple buck the Q2 global PC sales slump, which saw Apple enjoy a 13% year-over-year increase in shipments.

For the second-gen model, current expectations are for it to use the A19 processor, along with a potential 12GB of memory. It may also expand its color range.

items.title: iCloud's 'Anyone with the Link' option will trigger Apple content checks
items.content_html:
Apple will begin checking publicly shared iCloud links for harmful content with its 27.3 updates, with violations risking account bans or law enforcement referrals.

Apple will scan publicly linked iCloud content for harmful material starting with iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3. This includes content, such as photos and files, shared using "Anyone with the Link."

When a user shares content using Anyone with the Link, it removes end-to-end encryption. Apple states this is the case even if the owner or participants have enabled Advance Data Protection.

Apple can move, refuse, modify, or delete harmful content and take action against the owner's account. That can include disabling accounts, blocking replacement accounts tied to the same contact details, or contacting law enforcement if necessary.

This change does not apply to the "People you choose" setting, shared albums, or content simply uploaded into iCloud. It explicitly applies to content shared via Anyone with the Link.

items.title: New Bluetooth standard supports great lossless audio, but you'll need new headphones
items.content_html:
Bluetooth High Data Throughput will bring faster data transfers and higher quality audio than ever before, but it's more than a software update, it needs manufacturers to adopt it in hardware.

For something we all rely on for everything from external keyboards to wireless AirPods, Bluetooth can be closer to alchemy than a standard. But there is a Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) which organizes it, and which has now launched a new version that's faster and more capable.

"As the world's most widely used wireless standard, Bluetooth technology has continually evolved to meet the growing demands of an increasingly connected world," Neville Meijers, CEO of the Bluetooth SIG, said in a statement to AppleInsider. "The Bluetooth SIG member community has once again risen to the challenge."

"Bluetooth HDT brings a new level of performance to Bluetooth technology," he continued, "expanding the role it can play across consumer, commercial, and industrial markets and creating a powerful foundation for the next generation of wireless innovation."

Specifically, Bluetooth High Data Throughput (HDT) is an optional part of Bluetooth Core 7.0. Bluetooth HDT supports 7.5 Mbps, which is said to be almost four times faster than the current Bluetooth LE.

That speed opens up more possibilities than just transferring data faster so audio latency might be reduced, for instance. It means devices take less time to transmit more data so they use energy more efficiently.

Sounds good

The Bluetooth SIG says that the "flagship application" for the new standard will be premium wireless audio. Bluetooth HDT supports lossless and high-resolution audio, plus surround sound and spatial audio.

However, the fact that it is an optional part of the standard means that no one is actually required to adopt it. Since it will require new processors and is therefore an extra cost for manufacturers, it could take time for many of them to use it.

Which might just translate to manufacturers waiting to see what Apple does.

Apple has not publicly commented about adopting Bluetooth HDT. According to Japanese news site AV Watch, however, Bluetooth SIG has told local journalists that it is confident the standard will be adopted.

"[The decision] is left to each company," said Bluetooth SIG's chief marketing officer Ken Kolderup (in translation). "However, our current feeling is that [Apple's] interest is very high, because Apple executives are participating and we are currently discussing the standard."

Bluetooth SIG says that it expects to see Bluetooth HDT being supported in 2027.

items.title: macOS Golden Gate touch features work with external displays, Sidecar
items.content_html:
The new PROLED MacBook Pro isn't the only hardware that benefits from macOS Golden Gate's touch-centric changes. Third-party displays and Sidecar benefit from them too.

Apple's decision to bring touchscreen support to the new OLED-equipped MacBook Pro meant it had to also change macOS to work with it. However, the alterations won't be limited to just Apple's latest notebook launch at all.

Anyone using a touch-enabled external display will also be able to benefit from the new interface in macOS 27. That includes anyone that uses Sidecar with an iPad.

As for Sidecar on iPad, we've found that macOS touch enhancements work in the iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 developer betas.

We've tried it on two third-party touchscreen displays. It works on one out of the box, and not on the other at the moment. We've confirmed it's about drivers, and not about the display hardware, though.

Touching changes

While macOS Golden Gate looks normal in everyday use with a keyboard and trackpad or mouse, there are multiple small changes that apply when you use a touchscreen.

This includes the traffic light interface element in the top left of windows growing larger when touched, so they can be more easily touched by a finger. This is similar to the experience in iPadOS, with a single tap enlarging the tiny dots so your next tap can hit the right button with precision.

The top menu bars can also be dynamically enlarged to help with touch controls in the same way.

Long presses of a Dock icon or some other UI elements also brings up more touch-friendly menus and animations.

While the focus is on macOS itself, some of these changes will also apply to macOS apps immediately. Apple has said that gesture APIs can be used by developers to extend the touch support in their apps, beyond simple simulated mouse clicks.

Expansion was always expected

While you would expect Apple would want to keep new features to just the device it introduced them on at first, it is not the case here. Indeed, this isn't even Apple's first experience with making macOS more touch-friendly.

Sidecar has always allowed users to extend their Mac workspace to the iPad display. It even allowed users to control the screen with an Apple Pencil, but it didn't include an intuitive finger-based touch experience.

Yes, it worked, for things like multi-touch gestures, treating the iPad like a Magic Trackpad, but you didn't have any real interaction with the macOS interface itself.

As discovered during the initial developer betas of macOS 27 in June, Apple experimented with including better touch support in Sidecar. Anywhere you touched on the iPad display acted as a click of a mouse in the same region, with dragging also working too.

However, in the final implementation in macOS, Apple's tweaks to the interface makes it a lot easier to navigate macOS and its apps by touch alone.

items.title: What Google Maps looks like on both iPhone Duo displays, after upgrade
items.content_html:
The latest app to adapt to the new iPhone Duo is Google Maps, which now fills both displays to make maximum use of the device's screens. Here's what it looks like.

It's still early days for developers and the iPhone Duo, so it's still the case that very many iOS apps look poor on the new device. But those developers who weren't ready on day one, are now starting to support the benefits of the device.

Google Maps for iPhone has now been updated to version 26.44.4 expressly to add iPhone Duo support. As always, Google's App Store notes say only that the release features bug fixes, but if you're an existing user, you will see the real benefit immediately.

Previously, the outer screen had Google Maps slightly offset to the left, leaving room for the new iOS dock position. On the inside display, users got the regular iPhone app which could be moved to the left or right, but still left most of the screen unused.

Now both displays are full. It doesn't add very much to the outer display, although it's neater and very welcome.

On the inside, though, Google Maps is now this wide app with plenty of room for its menus and search box to the left. Now a map or satellite view fills the screen corner to corner, making it much more like Google Maps on the iPad.

Street View also benefits from the iPhone Duo's wider screen. Now by default, Street View takes up the left side of the screen, leaving the whole right for the map.

There doesn't appear to be a way to switch those to the opposite sides. However, Street View can be made to fill the entire screen, just as you readily can with Apple Maps's equivalent Look Around.

Closing the iPhone Duo while using Street View puts that part on the outer screen. But there is a close button that returns you to the map view.

Google Maps for iPhone is free on the App Store.

items.title: Apple's Lockdown Mode thwarted by a new persistent iPhone jailbreak
items.content_html:
A team of hackers has come up with a new jailbreak for the iPhone, demonstrating how it persists with Lockdown Mode on, even after an update to iOS 27.2.

Lockdown Mode is Apple's way to harden device security, intended to protect high-profile individuals from sophisticated cyberattacks. While Apple claimed back in March 2026 that it had managed a 100% protection rate since 2022, it seems it's not completely impenetrable.

In a video posted to X, hacker group Calif shows an iPhone 18 Pro with Lockdown Mode enabled. A PDF is then sent to the iPhone using AirDrop and viewed.

It is presumed that the PDF is part of the process, due to the change of music in the video. However, as Calif hasn't shared any technical details of the jailbreak in public, it could've been performed before the video started.

Lockdown Mode helps, until it doesn't. — Calif (@calif_io) November 3, 2026

Immediately after the AirDrop, the video shows someone navigating to the Software Update section of Settings, resulting in a pop-up warning Lockdown Mode is enabled and that it would affect certain settings. They then dismiss the notification, select to install the update to iOS 27.2, enter the iPhone's passcode, and allow the update to run.

After a few minutes, the iPhone processes the update and completes it successfully.

According to MacRumors, Calif has said it was disclosing found vulnerabilities to Apple. It also wasn't going to produce a jailbreak tool either.

A little less than perfect

If genuine, the video shows that Apple's Lockdown Mode is a secure way to protect your iPhone and your data from attacks, but not completely perfect.

The point of Lockdown Mode is that it hardens the iPhone's security for people who need it. Think politicians, activists, and CEOs who would be big targets for hackers.

Enabling Lockdown Mode in iOS 16 or later places many limits on apps and services operating on the iPhone. That includes blocking the use of some technologies while browsing the Internet and blocking links and most message types from being viewable in Messages.

On the more extreme end, it will block the installation of configuration mobiles, prevent the iPhone from being installed into Mobile Device Management systems, and will even disconnect from non-secure Wi-Fi networks.

The intention is to prevent many of the main avenues of attack that a hacker can use to access the target's on-device data and accounts.

The discovery of a jailbreak allowing an iOS update to occur while seemingly allowing the jailbreak to persist means Apple has more work to do.

Apple may have said in March that there had not been any successful hacks of iPhones in Lockdown Mode. Evidently that perfect record is blemished.

items.title: How USB-C drives can change how you use your iPhone
items.content_html:
The iPhone 15 family of devices was the first to have USB-C ports, but you really aren't making the most of it if all you do is use yours to charge. Here's what you can do, and what you can't with external drives.

The beauty of the USB-C port is that there are already countless devices and accessories out there that can plug into it. That's the benefit of a "universal" port, after all.

In the case of your iPhone, being able to charge it using a friend's cable is just the beginning. The real fun starts when you plug things like external storage into it.

But while taking a USB-C thumb drive and plugging it into your iPhone is certainly doable, how you can use it is more complicated. It also depends on exactly which iPhone you own as well.

Here, we're going to run down which iPhones are best suited to using USB-C storage, and why. We'll also get into why you might want to use a USB-C drive with your iPhone while detailing what it won't do, no matter how hard you try.

A pro feature for pro iPhones

While it's true that you can plug a USB-C storage device into any iPhone with a USB-C port, how fast it transfers data will depend on the iPhone itself.

The iPhone 15 and newer non-Pro iPhones all have USB 2.0 ports, so they're limited to data transfer speeds of just 480Mbps, or around 50MB/s. That includes the iPhone Air.

This limitation may also have a larger impact than just making you wait longer for files to transfer. Accessing some files directly from a USB-C drive at USB 2.0 speeds could have its own problems.

One example would be playing back video files. Depending on the quality of the video, USB 2.0 speeds may simply be too slow to reliably stream the video from the drive.

In such cases, you can always copy the video to your iPhone before watching it. But that does rely on you having the time to wait for the copy and the space on your iPhone, too.

The iPhone 15 Pro and newer, plus the iPhone Duo, all have USB 3 ports capable of data transfer speeds of 10Gbps. That works out to around 1,000 MB/s.

If your iPhone has one of those USB 3 ports, you can plug in a high-speed portable SSD to expand your storage. But don't expect your iPhone to treat that SSD as if it were internal storage, because it's more complicated than that.

What you can use external storage for

With Apple keeping the top-speed USB-C ports back for the Pro iPhones, it's no surprise that some of the most notable use cases are for creative professionals.

Direct ProRes video recording

When connected to an iPhone that supports it, high-bitrate ProRes video recording supports up to 4K capture at 60 and 120 fps directly to an external SSD. There's a very good reason, too, in that ProRes files can be extremely large.

There are different options available when choosing to record in ProRes. But as a primer, 4K ProRes video recorded on an iPhone can use up to 6GB of storage for every minute of video captured.

That's why Apple limits the higher-quality ProRes capture settings to those iPhones with an external SSD plugged in. In those cases, the ProRes files are written directly to that SSD to save internal storage space.

File management and media transfer

The built-in Files app supports external SSDs, and you can move, copy, rename, view, and organize files at will. You can access files directly from the portable SSD itself, while you can also move files to and from it as well.

This approach can be useful if you need to access and work with large files, such as videos. But it can also be a great way to move data between devices without relying on AirDrop or other file transfer mechanisms.

The Files app is a great way to move and manage files on an iPhone.

Media playback

You can plug an external SSD into your iPhone and play back media that is saved on it. The most obvious example here is movies and TV shows, but high-resolution photos will also work.

How you access your media may depend on which app you plan to use. Some apps, like Infuse, have their own file managers that allow you to open files directly from within them.

Another option would be to use the Files app. Tap and hold a media file, then tap Open In before selecting the app you'd like to use.

This is a reliable way to access large media files without them taking up valuable space on your iPhone's internal, often limited, storage.

Manual data backup

Whether you use the Files app or file management features built into your favorite apps, an external SSD is an excellent way to back up data.

While iCloud backups help preserve the data on your iPhone, that isn't always ideal. Such data is then locked within a backup on Apple's iCloud servers and not readily accessible.

Instead, you can use the Files app to manually back up any important data and files to an external SSD. Some USB sticks and drives also have iPhone apps that can be used to automatically back up photos, videos, and contact data.

Backing data up to an external SSD means you maintain control and can access that data from other devices if the need ever arises.

What you CAN'T use external storage for

For every useful way an external SSD can upgrade your iPhone-using experience, there are plenty more that simply won't. Apple still keeps iOS locked down in plenty of ways, and that includes the way external storage can be used.

Installing apps

You might think that you'd be able to combine your new external storage with your iPhone's internal storage to install more apps. Unfortunately, that isn't the case.

Apps can only be installed on an iPhone's internal storage.

Apple prevents apps from being installed anywhere other than the iPhone's internal storage. If you want more space for apps, you'll need to buy a bigger capacity when it's time for a new iPhone.

There are a few reasons why this is the case. Apple would argue that installing apps on external storage would open the door to potential piracy and data privacy issues, for example.

Automated system backups

While you can back up some data to an external SSD via the Files app and in-app data management features, wholesale backups are out of the question.

Apple does not allow full iPhone backups to be made to external storage. Instead, they're limited to iCloud backups to Apple servers and backups that are made over a cable to a Mac or PC.

None of these automated backups can be rerouted to an external SSD, as useful as that may be.

Direct standard Camera app recording

Capturing Apple ProRes video to an external SSD is a great option, and it's required for the higher-resolution options. But the ability to save videos to external storage doesn't extend to standard formats.

Normal camera modes, including standard H.264/HEVC video capture, Time-Lapse, Slo-Mo, and Photo mode, save directly to internal storage. Files generated from these features cannot be saved to an external SSD when they are created.

Encrypted data access

Given Apple's stance on privacy and encryption, it's unfortunate that not all encrypted drives can be used with an iPhone. APFS (Encrypted)-formatted drives can be accessed, as can drives that have a physical keypad for decryption or offer a companion iOS app.

However, drives that use software-based encryption designed for Windows, like BitLocker, will not work correctly. Neither will third-party solutions that don't have their own companion iOS app.

USB-C has always been more than a charging port

When Apple added USB-C to the iPhone, most people saw it as a way to use one charging cable for multiple devices. And while that's a key benefit, it isn't the only one.

For a lot of people, being able to connect a USB-C drive, whether that's an SSD or a thumb drive, is huge. Just remember that you'll need an iPhone Pro or an iPhone Duo to get the most out of it.

items.title: iPhone 18 rumored to get larger battery, higher price
items.content_html:
A repetitive but generally reliable leaker has listed specifications for the forthcoming iPhone 18, and one significant update may be increased battery life.

Leaker Digital Chat Station has recently taken to reposting previous rumors as new, including ones about the iPhone 18e. Much of their latest report is, again, a repeat, but it does add that the battery life will be extended.

The post is written on the Chinese social media site Weibo and this detail about the battery comes at the end of a short list of iPhone 18 specifications:

  • 6.3-inch 1.5K 120Hz OLED
  • Regular Dynamic Island (not the smaller new one)
  • 2nm A20 processor
  • Face ID
  • 48MP dual-camera system

There are no specifications given for the battery size, so it's possible that this is just reasonable speculation. Apple generally increases battery capacity each year, as it has done most recently with the iPhone 18 Pro.

Similarly, the iPhone 17 had a larger battery than the iPhone 16. However, that was due in part to Apple using the space previously taken by a physical SIM card, so there won't be the same option again.

The new leak also says that the price of the iPhone 18 is likely to be higher than its predecessor, the iPhone 17. That again could be just informed speculation, though.

Nonetheless, the leaker predicts that the iPhone 18 will be a big seller. They don't appear to have based this on accounts of Apple's orders, though, so yet again this may be just reasonable expectation.

items.title: macOS Golden Gate touch features work with external displays, Sidecar
items.content_html:
The new PROLED MacBook Pro isn't the only hardware that benefits from macOS Golden Gate's touch-centric changes. Third-party displays and Sidecar benefit from them too.

Touching the traffic light buttons in macOS Golden Gate, using an iPad with Sidecar

Apple's decision to bring touchscreen support to the new OLED-equipped MacBook Pro meant it had to also change macOS to work with it. However, the alterations won't be limited to just Apple's latest notebook launch at all.

Anyone using a touch-enabled external display will also be able to benefit from the new interface in macOS 27. That includes anyone that uses Sidecar with an iPad.

As for Sidecar on iPad, we've found that macOS touch enhancements work in the iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 developer betas.

We've tried it on two third-party touchscreen displays. It works on one out of the box, and not on the other at the moment. We've confirmed it's about drivers, and not about the display hardware, though.

Touching changes

While macOS Golden Gate looks normal in everyday use with a keyboard and trackpad or mouse, there are multiple small changes that apply when you use a touchscreen.

This includes the traffic light interface element in the top left of windows growing larger when touched, so they can be more easily touched by a finger. This is similar to the experience in iPadOS, with a single tap enlarging the tiny dots so your next tap can hit the right button with precision.

Watch: macOS Golden Gate touch features demo

The top menu bars can also be dynamically enlarged to help with touch controls in the same way.

Long presses of a Dock icon or some other UI elements also brings up more touch-friendly menus and animations.

While the focus is on macOS itself, some of these changes will also apply to macOS apps immediately. Apple has said that gesture APIs can be used by developers to extend the touch support in their apps, beyond simple simulated mouse clicks.

Expansion was always expected

While you would expect Apple would want to keep new features to just the device it introduced them on at first, it is not the case here. Indeed, this isn't even Apple's first experience with making macOS more touch-friendly.

Sidecar has always allowed users to extend their Mac workspace to the iPad display. It even allowed users to control the screen with an Apple Pencil, but it didn't include an intuitive finger-based touch experience.

Yes, it worked, for things like multi-touch gestures, treating the iPad like a Magic Trackpad, but you didn't have any real interaction with the macOS interface itself.

As discovered during the initial developer betas of macOS 27 in June, Apple experimented with including better touch support in Sidecar. Anywhere you touched on the iPad display acted as a click of a mouse in the same region, with dragging also working too.

However, in the final implementation in macOS, Apple's tweaks to the interface makes it a lot easier to navigate macOS and its apps by touch alone.

Read on AppleInsider

items.title: Apple Music gaining new Selfie Sing video karaoke mode
items.content_html:
Starting in iOS 27.3, Apple Music users will be able to capture videos of themselves singing songs along to the lyrics thanks to a new Selfie Sing feature.

Apple is expanding its Apple Music feature set with more karaoke-like options. Apple Music Sing already let users turn down vocals and sing along with the highlighted lyrics, but a new mode brings them into the mix.

The Selfie Sing feature exists in the iOS 27.3 beta and was first shared by code sleuth Aaron Perris. While his video shows an Animoji, that isn't a feature of Selfie Sing, just an effort to avoid posting a video of himself singing.

Sorry, no official Animoji Karaoke here, but this does mean it's only one step away.

The feature is only available on iPhones even though the special Selfie Sing playlist will show up for anyone. An iPad Pro running iPadOS 27.3 doesn't provide an option to use the camera.

When a song is playing that works with Selfie Sing is playing on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, a new camera toggle will appear under the vocal audio volume control. Tapping this will take you into a video recording feature that only produces vertical video.

It also works with iPhone Duo's rear-camera-as-a-selfie-camera mode by moving the video capture to the outer display. This gives the user a chance to capture the video with the best cameras while still being able to see the on-screen lyrics.

Apple has tried to implement social media-friendly features like this before, but via the Clips app. Having it baked into Apple Music could prove to be a fun gimmick if it catches on among social media users.

However, like "slofies" there is a good chance this Selfie Sing feature falls to the background. It's a cute, if limited karaoke feature that once again feels more tailored for the pandemic era.

items.title: Apple officially restricts employee participation in prediction markets
items.content_html:
If you're an Apple employee or contractor planning to make money using insider information to gamble in legally-gray "prediction markets," don't. Apple has made its stance clear in a new filing.

Prediction markets skirt the legal definition of gambling, which means they have become widely available in the United States in spite of gambling laws. These markets can be used to bet on everything from when a location might see its first snow to what colors the latest iPhones will be sold in.

Regardless of the legality of these markets, Apple has made it clear that using insider information to participate is considered insider trading. While the companies like Polymarket already have insider trading rules, these enable Apple to act against violators from their end.

The text is explicit and leaves no wiggle room:

"No Trading in Prediction Markets Based on Confidential Information. Do not participate in 'prediction markets' or similar platforms to wager, bet, trade, buy or sell contracts based on the outcome of future events, or otherwise enter into event contracts, when such activity involves the use of Apple Confidential Information (as defined in Apple's Business Conduct Policy) about Apple or any other company (including Apple suppliers, manufacturers, vendors or customers, such as cellular network carriers or other business partners) obtained in connection with your work at Apple."

"You must also not tip Apple Confidential Information to others who may participate in such markets. Apple Confidential Information includes, but is not limited to, material nonpublic information.

This prohibition applies whether or not the activity constitutes insider trading or securities trading under applicable laws."

The emergence of prediction markets has created a new avenue for mass fraud and insider trading. The technology to easily participate in such betting pools advanced faster than the laws and regulations can be written, so it has fallen to individual companies to attempt to police these things on their own.

These rules extend to employees that have left Apple or have been fired. All protections against insider trading extend to information that ties to unreleased or unannounced products.

Once a product, service, or update has been revealed, the restrictions are lifted. Then, of course, it is public knowledge and there is nothing left to bet on.

items.title: Hands on: iOS 27.3 beta's Safari, Siri AI, vertical tabs, and more
items.content_html:
Apple has shared the first beta of iOS 27.3, which brings back the redesigned Apple Health app and several new features for testing. Here's what's new.

Apple was stung by overpromising and underdelivering with its infamous WWDC 2024 where Apple Intelligence was first announced. While many new features were revealed during WWDC 2026, many showing up in later betas are being revealed for the first time.

The first beta for iOS 27.3 brings back the redesigned Apple Health app, plus introduces all-new features that were previously not announced. AppleInsider staff has updates installed on across their iPhones, iPads, Macs, and Apple Watches to try them all out and see what else is new.

There were already surprising new additions with iOS 27.2, such as Dual Capture for FaceTime, Multi-View for iPhone, Apple TV profiles on iPhone and iPad, just to name a few.

Several of Apple's first-party apps have been updated alongside new Siri AI features. Let's get into what's new.

Safari

Out of the gate, one of the best new additions is a slew of improvements to Safari. Apple has added an option for vertical tabs, an AI-powered Adaptive Dark Mode, and new Siri AI capabilities.

The new Adaptive Dark Mode is available on iPhone and Mac.

Vertical tabs are a recent fad in browsers and their addition to Safari makes things look cleaner than before. They support Apple's prior features like Tab Groups, and when you hover over the site icon, it will show the full site name.

The new vertical tabs work on Safari for iPhone Duo, which takes perfect advantage of the wider display.

Adaptive Dark Mode uses Apple Intelligence to analyze sites that don't natively support Dark Mode. It will darken backgrounds, adjust text contrast, invert logos and graphics, recolor vector artwork, and rebalance layered shadows.

We've tested this on a few sites that currently don't natively support a dark interface, and it works quite well. Devs still retain control of this with the ability to block Adaptive Dark Mode, but we think this will make browsing Safari at night much more comfortable.

Siri AI is much more powerful with this update, too. It now understands an entire webpage, can search amongst your open tabs, take actions on your tabs, and manage your browsing history.

Localization has been improved as well, with Siri AI now available in Norwegian, Traditional Chinese, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

If you are looking at a long, detailed product page on the new Apple Watch, you could ask Siri AI to find the weight difference between the aluminum and titanium models. You could also ask it to organize your tabs or clear a site from your history in the past week.

The new Health app returns

After briefly popping up in the iOS 27.2 beta cycle, Apple's redesigned Health app is back. The new app has a fresh layout, an AI-enhanced health summary, and in-app tests that you can do to help measure your overall wellness.

The redesigned Apple Health app has arrived with iOS 27.3, and language support has improved.

It adds a Longevity tab to the app with your health summary broken down into different categories like food and sleep. If you were testing this before, your data will carry over to the new testing period.

Besides your overall health, it gives you your "Health Age." This looks at your health and tells you how old your body is in comparison to your physical age.

The redesigned Apple Health app also expands language support. In addition to English, it's available in Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

Apple still says the redesigned Apple Health app will arrive later in 2026 without making promises about which version of iOS. It may be included in the final release of iOS 27.3, but that hasn't been confirmed.

Siri Recap & Live Rewind

Two flagship features of Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12 have officially entered beta. They are the Audio Intelligence features called Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Siri Recap is finally here with iOS 27.3. Image Credit: Apple

Apple says that Siri Recap will automatically detect conversations throughout your day and provide helpful summaries within the Siri app. These are meant to be private by design, and no audio is ever saved or recorded.

It takes things like speaker proximity, duration, and more into consideration when detecting these conversations. The summary will give you the high points of what was discussed with no speaker attribution, and the summaries are automatically deleted from the Siri app if they're not saved.

Users can decide when this feature is active, including by limiting it to times of day and location. For example, you could just use it when you are at work and turn it off when you're home, or enable it during the day but turn it off after 8 PM.

The other feature, called Live Rewind, is activated with a double-press of the Digital Crown on your Apple Watch. It gives you a transcription of what was said in the last 15 seconds, though it does not name the speaker.

When enabled, the entire screen of the Apple Watch lights up, and it audibly chimes so it's visibly and audibly clear that it was enabled. Once more, there are no recordings saved and all the processing is done locally on your devices.

It remains to be seen exactly how useful these features might be, especially in circumstances where the user can ask the speaker to repeat themselves. Both may be too invasive for some to consider enabling.

Siri AI is now more capable than ever

With the first iOS 27.3 beta, Apple gave Siri AI additional in-app actions, available in the Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather applications.

iOS 27.3 makes Siri AI much more useful.

These new options are easy to discover, too. You can ask Siri AI what it can do in supported apps to discover new capabilities.

In Apple Music, for instance, Siri AI can create and save playlists. In Calendar app, Siri AI can now schedule appointments with other people, while including locations and call links.

Siri AI can also unsubscribe users from mailing lists, and un-send recently sent emails in the Mail application.

Meanwhile, in Safari, Siri AI can be used to close tabs or manage tabs outright, clear the user's browser history, or to add an article to the user's Reading List. It is also capable of scheduling messages, opening files, and much more.

The new personalized feature can also tap into your location history, when necessary. It can find, for instance, the coffee shop you visited last week and display it in Apple Maps.

These various features have been long-awaited by those that have had initial issues with the new Siri AI. The Apple Music features, for example, were basically broken before.

Gym Strength in Apple Fitness+

In addition to the revamped Apple Health app, iOS 27.3 introduces Gym Strength. It's an all-new program for Apple Fitness+ subscribers that delivers personalized workout plans focused on strength training.

iOS 27.3 brings Gym Strength, albeit only for Apple Fitness+ subscribers.

The custom four-week programs generated with Gym Strength will take into account your experience level, equipment preferences, schedule, and more. In short, it will help you train, even if you have no experience, virtually no equipment, and even if you can only train a couple of days a week.

According to Apple, you'll be able to choose from more than 350 exercises. One Gym Strength workout consists of five to seven exercises, totalling anywhere from 20 to 60 minutes, depending on your preferences.

You'll also get access to video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers, which will come in handy if you haven't used strength training equipment before.

These demonstrations will show you how to use dumbbells, barbells, kettlebells, and much more. Over 30 types of training equipment are featured.

You can even log your Gym Strength workouts on an Apple Watch, and the data can be used to customize next week's exercises. The app will recommend what exercises to do, including how many reps and sets, and how much weight to set.

Gym Strength is part of the Fitness+ subscription, which costs $9.99 per month or $79.99 per year on its own, or as part of the $39.95 Apple One Premier plan.

Other new features and changes

Those are the biggest features Apple introduced with iOS 27.3, but they're by no means the only changes. For instance, Apple improved the customization options for clock faces in StandBy mode.

iOS 27.3 brings StandBy clock faces previously limited to the iPhone Duo to more iPhone models.

In short, this means that owners of all iPhones running iOS 27.3 will get the new clock faces, colors, and complications available on the iPhone Duo. The foldable itself, meanwhile, has gained the horizontal Reachability feature that was touted in October 2026.

With iOS 27.3, Reachability can shift the left or right side of the screen to the other side with a short swipe. This makes every part of the UI accessible from one hand, while also holding the iPhone Duo itself. The feature is available within the Settings app, under Accessibility, followed by Reachability.

In the Apple Music app, a new splash screen highlights improvements to Auto Mix, the Concerts For You feature, and redesigned Artist Pages featuring custom visuals.

Separately, Apple Intelligence is now available in beta to users in China, though that does not extend to Siri AI. Features like the Clean Up tool in Photos, along with Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence, however, are all usable in China.

As for iPad users, iPadOS 27.3 brings Apple's new Siri Mode to the Camera app. The software update also makes the Apple Pencil usable with Visual Intelligence. macOS Golden Gate, meanwhile, has also received Safari's new Adaptive Dark mode.

Overall, Tuesday's developer betas are packed full of new features, and iOS 27.3 is shaping up to be a huge upgrade. Though we're still at the start of the beta testing cycle, iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 are expected to receive a full public release in December 2026.

items.title: If schools turn off Google's AI, Search dies with it
items.content_html:
Google's response to criticism of AI use in classrooms gives schools a choice with a catch: rejecting Gemini also means cutting off student access to Google Search.

Google announced Tuesday that its AI services would be disabled by default for school-managed K-12 student accounts. There's a big catch to that, though.

Schools that leave Gemini disabled will also lose Google Search access for those accounts.

The change will affect Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search, extending beyond Google Classroom itself. Google cited AI's growing integration into Search and said administrators must explicitly enable access.

Previously, Gemini was activated automatically for schools using Google Classroom, drawing criticism from senators and advocacy groups. As NBC notes, more than a dozen parent advocacy organizations urged districts to disable Gemini and YouTube over concerns about student use in October.

Requiring schools to opt in technically gives advocacy groups what they're asking for. However, prohibiting Google Search is a clear attempt to strong-arm schools into using AI products.

In an attempt to assuage parents' and teachers' fears, and try to convince the to leave Gemini on, Google is expanding its "Guided Learning" feature. Guided Learning is an interactive AI tutoring mode in Gemini designed to function as a study partner for students.

What Guided Learning does not do, and probably won't, is teach critical thinking. What it does not do, is teach students how to effectively search for information.

There's no media literacy in Guided Learning. And most importantly, Guided Learning does not teach the student how to find multiple, accurate sources to draw an independent conclusion.

Google plans to bring Guided Learning to Search in the coming months. The company says it will guide students through certain homework problems instead of giving them answers.

We are incredibly skeptical that there is value here for students, parents, or educators.

items.title: Apple Intelligence arrives in China via iOS 27.3 developer beta
items.content_html:
After two years of waiting, the first iOS 27.3 developer beta has introduced Apple Intelligence to China, bringing some of its AI features to the country.

Apple Intelligence will finally ship in China - Image Credit: Apple

The long wait for Apple Intelligence in China started in 2024 after its introduction in the U.S. Two years later, and after Apple confirmed its impending arrival on Saturday, Apple Intelligence is now making an officially sanctioned appearance in China.

Rolling out as part of the iOS 27.3 developer beta, the first wave won't be the full Apple Intelligence experience. Instead it will mirror a lot of the earlier incarnations of Apple Intelligence.

Those initial features include tools for Photos, including Clean Up to eliminate unwanted items from images, as well as memory videos and natural language search. There's also Visual Intelligence using the iPhone camera and smart emoji generation.

Writing tools are also present, complete with options to proofread, rewrite, and summarize text. It can also generate notification summaries and email summaries.

Smart Reply will quickly suggest responses to messages. Meanwhile, Notes gains audio transcription, and calls can get transcribed and summarized.

The update stops short of adding Siri AI, which only became available to users in other countries in 2026.

Getting Apple Intelligence to the iPhone has been difficult for Apple, due to Chinese regulations. It had to seek out various local partners who had approved models it could use for the same services.

In its announcement, Apple says it uses generative models built by Apple, and is also working with Alibaba to add Qianwen support within Siri.

Apple plans to properly launch Apple Intelligence in China with iOS 27.3's public release in December.

items.title: Elgato's new teleprompter app follows your voice & doesn't need special hardware
items.content_html:
Elgato's Virtual Prompter doesn't need special hardware, and follows your voice as you read, keeping scripts near your webcam during presentations, recordings, and video calls.

On Tuesday, Elgato announced Virtual Prompter, a new feature in Elgato Studio that turns your computer screen into a teleprompter without external hardware requirements. There are two modes that users can utilize: docked or floating.

Docked places the script in a strip along the top of your screen near your camera, perfect for maintaining eye contact while reading. Docked is free to use and has no time limits.

Floating lets users put scripts in a window they can move, resize, or take full screen on another display. It requires Virtual Prompter Pro.

Both modes have the same script-scrolling options: set your script to scroll at a set speed or follow your voice with Voice Sync. Voice Sync listens through the microphone, scrolls as you speak, and follows if you skip a line.

Users can write in Elgato Studio, paste text from elsewhere. They can also import documents, including Word, Markdown, and plain text files.

If you stream, a helpful chat mode shows Twitch, YouTube, or Kick chat in the same spot.

Virtual Prompter Pro costs $2.99 per month or $29.90 per year; you can also purchase a lifetime license for $49.99. However, Elgato Prompter and Prompter XL owners get free use while their hardware is connected.

Virtual Prompter is available for both Windows and Mac as part of Elgato Studio 2.0, available to download here. Mac users will need to run macOS 15 Sequoia or later.

items.title: Apple brings 3 big new features to Safari on iPhone, iPad, & Mac in initial 27.3 beta
items.content_html:
Apple has released the first developer betas of 27.3 and Safari is getting three new features: vertical tabs, adaptive dark mode, and more Siri AI.

The 27.3 update is looking like a huge one for Apple, with new features across all of Apple's platforms. The new Health app has made its return, Apple Watch is getting new Siri AI features, and Apple Intelligence is coming to China.

Then we have Safari on iPhone, iPad, and Mac that is seeing a trio of substantial new features.

Vertical tabs

The first addition to Safari is vertical tabs, which even works on iPhone Duo. It looks incredible and is a long-requested feature from users.

Vertical tabs come to iPhone Duo, iPad, and Mac with their respective 27.3 updates

It's quicker to scan full tab titles and it's more space-efficient for displaying content. To enable, users can turn on Vertical Tabs from the View menu on the Mac and iPad or within the dedicated Safari settings on iPhone.

Adaptive Dark Mode

Apple has supported Dark Mode for years, and there is even an automatic version that switches your device in the evening. Some people prefer the aesthetic but Dark Mode is also easier on the eyes in dim environments.

Adaptive Dark Mode options within Safari in macOS 27.3

If you've ever been browsing Safari late at night only to have a bright white background sear your eyes, you know why Dark Mode exists. Many websites have custom styling that follows your device's appearance settings and goes between a light and dark styling.

Some sites though, have not done the legwork and do not support a dark appearance. Starting with the 27.3 updates, iPhone, iPad, and Mac will have Adaptive Dark Mode that intelligently changes these sites to be darker.

Adaptive Dark Mode on and off

The feature uses Apple Intelligence to analyze each site you visit individually. When you first visit a site that could benefit from Adaptive Dark Mode, an alert will appear at the top of the page prompting you to enable it.

Adaptive Dark Mode will darken light backgrounds, tune the text contrast, invert logos and graphics as needed, recolor vector artwork, and rebalances layered shadows on complex layouts.

Developers still have full control of the and there is a tag that they can add that will force the site to appear as-is if they do not want Adaptive Dark Mode to apply to their site. This is also a beta, so it will likely change and improve throughout the beta cycle.

Siri AI expands

Finally, Apple is adding additional support for Siri AI within Safari. It has additional context and expanded controls across tabs and content.

When viewing a page, Siri AI understands the entirety of the page. For example, if you're looking at a long product item description, you could ask Siri AI how heavy the item is and it would search the page for its weight.

Siri AI can now take action across tabs too, such as "put all these tabs into one group" or "close all my Reddit tabs." You could ask Siri AI to "clear my history of this site within the last 20 days."

Coming soon

The new features currently in beta will likely ship with iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3, though there is always a chance they will be delayed. The suite of 27.3 updates will arrive to users in December.

Some features will also come to Safari 27.3 for macOS Tahoe, though Adaptive Dark Mode and Siri AI will require an Apple Intelligence device.

items.title: First developer betas of iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3 arrive for testing
items.content_html:
Following the release of the 27.2 operating system updates, Apple has started the developer beta process for iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and others.

Apple concluded its most recent developer beta process for the 27.2 range of operating systems in late October. Following the public releases, Apple has embarked on a whole new beta round.

The first developer builds of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3 Golden Gate, watchOS 27.3, visionOS 27.3, and tvOS 27.3 are now available for testing.

The first builds are:

  • iOS 27.3 beta 1 is 24C5037i
  • iPadOS 27.3 beta 1 is 24C5037i
  • macOS 27.3 beta 1 is 26C5035r
  • tvOS 27.3 beta 1 is 24K5286g
  • watchOS 27.3 beta 1 is 24S5284h
  • visionOS 27.3 beta 1 is 24N5286r
  • HomePod Software 27.3 beta 1 is 24K5286g

At the same time, Apple has also introduced two update release candidates for older macOS versions:

  • macOS 26.7.3 RC 1 is 25G416
  • macOS 15.8.2 RC 1 is 24H314

At this early stage, it is unclear what the main content of the 27.3 updates will be, but online sleuths will be examining the builds and searching out clues in the hours after their introduction.

As always, AppleInsider warns readers not to use developer beta software on primary or mission-critical systems, unless absolutely necessary. Ideally, they should do so only with adequate backups of their data on hand, and ideally on secondary non-essential devices.

Members of the public are usually better suited to trying out the public betas.

Find any changes in the new builds? Reach out to us on X at @AppleInsider or @Andrew_OSU, or send Andrew an email at andrew@appleinsider.com.

items.title: Siri AI will not get real chatbots until Apple can secure them
items.content_html:
John Ternus is definitely on board with adding agentic tools to Siri AI - image background credit: Apple.

John Ternus has said that Apple wants Siri AI to offer agentic AI tools, but not until it can be sure users truly understand what the risks are.

The world's first real exposure to AI came with OpenAI's chatbot, ChatGPT. When many other firms then released their own chatbots, Apple was regarded as being behind on AI because it didn't have one.

Today AI, at least for the aficionados Apple's Greg Joswiak calls the "lunatic fringe," technology has moved on. Agentic AI is arguably the buzzword now, with AI tools able to take action on users' computers to, for instance, send messages or build apps.

Apple still has neither an AI agent nor a chatbot, or at least not for consumers, and John Ternus believes that's right. Speaking on Apple's latest earnings call he denied that Apple was against AI agents.

"As far as agentic capabilities, you know, we think these are promising tools for users," he said. "We just want to make sure that users are aware of what they're giving access to."

"We want to make sure this is done in a way that protects security and privacy," he continued.

Siri AI is not agentic, is not a chatbot

Siri AI is much better at many things than its Siri predecessor, including the ability to have a kind of conversation with it. But Apple believes that remembering context does not make Siri AI into a chatbot, and that it shouldn't.

"If you use many of the existing chatbots, they're really focused on engagement to a large degree, and sycophancy, right? They kind of want to pull you in," Apple's Craig Federighi said in June 2026. "They might encourage you to reveal things about yourself and then use that as a basis to establish a connection."

"The way that we have designed Siri," he continued, "Siri really wants to say, 'Listen, that's not what I'm here for, I'm here to help you.' [If] you try to engage Siri as a romantic partner, Siri's not into that."

So while others may call Siri AI a chatbot and it is much more of one in this new version than it was before, Apple doesn't see it that way. Now based on Ternus's few remarks during the earnings call, it seems clear that Apple is approaching agentic AI with the same specific aim.

Users come first

Apple appears to believe that users should not have to regard Siri AI as a chatbot, they should just know what it can do for them when they ask. Similarly, Apple believes that users shouldn't have to worry about AI agents.

Right now there is plenty to worry about and it concerns what Ternus said about access. Users aren't always told, or just don't always know, exactly what they are risking giving up when they use today's agents.

"With Siri AI, we really have the kind of the Siri that we always wanted," said Ternus during the earnings call. "It's primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it's built on a modern orchestrated-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand its capabilities over time."

"So, you know, we're pushing really hard on [privacy and security] with Siri AI," he continued.

Apple already has the most private of all the AI services, and that's increasingly becoming a selling point of its devices. If it can find a way to give users agentic tools that remain private, Apple could cement its place as where users don't have to think or worry about AI.

It could cement its place as where users only need to know what their devices can do for them, not whether something is an AI feature or not.

Apple definitely sees AI and its hardware as forever connected, too. "[We're] also really encouraged the fact that Apple devices, we think, are the best places to use all forms of AI," concluded Ternus.

items.title: How to replace your Mac's speakers with a HomePod stereo pair
items.content_html:
Compatible HomePods can now handle Mac system sounds through a persistent AirPlay connection designed to reduce delays. Here's how to set one or a pair as your Mac's default speakers, and how well it works.

Mac owners have long streamed music to HomePods, but traditional AirPlay's delay makes it less practical for games, video calls, and other apps. Apple's latest update aims to make HomePods useful as everyday Mac speakers, not just for music.

The feature arrived with macOS 27.2 and HomePod software 27.2 on October 26, 2026. Apple describes it as a responsive, persistent AirPlay connection that lets compatible HomePods handle a Mac's audio without repeatedly establishing a new stream.

For anyone who already has a HomePod sitting near their Mac, it's a potentially useful alternative to buying separate desktop speakers. However, getting music to play through a HomePod doesn't necessarily mean the new connection is working.

Which Macs and HomePods support persistent audio

The persistent AirPlay connection supports the following HomePod models, either individually or as stereo pairs:

  • Second-generation HomePod
  • HomePod mini 2

The original HomePod and first-generation HomePod mini still support conventional AirPlay, but they can't establish the newer persistent connection.

Your Mac must also support Wi-Fi 6E or newer, with compatible models introduced in 2023 or later including:

  • M3 MacBook Air and later
  • MacBook Neo
  • MacBook Pro
  • iMac
  • Mac mini
  • Mac Studio
  • Mac Pro

The hardware requirement is important because installing macOS 27.2 on an older Mac doesn't automatically enable the feature. You don't need a Wi-Fi 6E router, however, since the requirement concerns the Mac's and HomePod's wireless hardware.

A stereo pair is another option if you want separate left and right audio channels at your desk.

A stereo pair is another option if you want separate left and right audio channels at your desk. Both HomePods must be the same model and configured as a stereo pair through Apple's Home app before selecting them on the Mac.

How to set a HomePod as your Mac's default speaker

Before configuring audio, make sure your HomePod is set up in the Home app and running software version 27.2 or later. You'll also need macOS 27.2 or newer, which you can check under System Settings, General, Software Update.

Once both devices meet those requirements, macOS lets you choose the HomePod as an audio output device.

  1. Open System Settings on your Mac and select Sound from the sidebar.
  2. Under Output, find your HomePod or stereo pair in the list of available audio devices.
  3. Select the HomePod to route your Mac's audio through it.
  4. Find the Sound Effects section and open the Play sound effects through menu.
  5. If AirPlay appears as an option, select it to send system sound effects to the HomePod.
  6. Choose an alert sound to preview it and check whether the audio comes from the HomePod rather than your Mac's built-in speakers.

macOS can send system alerts to a different speaker from music and other audio. Even when music plays through your HomePod, notifications may still come from the Mac's built-in speakers.

How to set a HomePod as your Mac's default speaker

On a supported configuration, the AirPlay option should become available for system sound effects when a compatible HomePod is selected. It's a useful indication that the newer functionality is available, although it doesn't establish how reliably the connection will perform.

Play and pause a video to check for audio delays, then try a system alert. You can also put your Mac to sleep and wake it again to see whether the HomePod remains selected as the audio output.

Apple intends the persistent connection to keep HomePod available for Mac audio without the repeated manual selection associated with traditional AirPlay.

What to do if HomePod won't play system sounds

Apple Music can stream to a HomePod through traditional AirPlay, so hearing music through the speaker doesn't confirm the new persistent connection is working. In our testing with an M3 MacBook Air and HomePod mini 2, music played through the HomePod while system alerts still came from the Mac.

If you encounter similar behavior, return to System Settings, Sound, and check both the selected output device and the "Play sound effects through" setting.

If AirPlay isn't available for system effects, confirm that your hardware is supported and both devices are running the required software. The HomePod may still appear as an ordinary AirPlay destination, even though the persistent connection isn't available.

Is using a HomePod as a Mac speaker worth it?

If you already own compatible HomePods, you can use them as Mac speakers without adding more equipment to your desk. The HomePod mini 2 takes up little space, while a stereo pair delivers wider sound without extra cables connecting the speakers to your Mac.

HomePods retain their normal smart-speaker features when connected to a Mac, including Siri voice commands, smart-home controls, timers, and Intercom. However, Siri interactions may interrupt Mac audio playback or cause the Mac to switch back to its built-in speakers, so the persistent connection's behavior during voice commands is worth checking.

Apple intends the persistent connection to keep HomePod available for Mac audio.

Our speaker comparison examines the differences between the HomePod mini 2 and the original model. It covers audio performance and the new Mac connectivity features.

In our testing, the HomePod mini 2 delivered clear, balanced audio, and there wasn't a noticeable difference in audio quality compared to the original mode. It filled the room evenly regardless of placement, with plenty of volume for comfortable listening.

HomePods are designed to fill a room with sound, which isn't always ideal in a shared workspace. Other people may hear your notifications and meeting audio, so headphones are a better choice when you need privacy.

The feature also handles audio output, not every part of a Mac's sound configuration. You'll still need to check the separate Input setting when using FaceTime or another calling application, rather than assuming the HomePod's microphones will replace the Mac's microphone.

Wired speakers still offer more consistent audio timing, especially if the HomePod's persistent AirPlay connection isn't working reliably.

If you mostly listen to music, conventional AirPlay may be all you need. The new connection is more useful as it, so far, reliably handles system alerts, calls, and other interactive audio.

items.title: iPhone 18e isn't going to get a dramatic overhaul
items.content_html:
The iPhone 18e will be a lot like the iPhone 17e with very few changes, with a switch from the notch to Dynamic Island probably not coming this time around.

Apple has a tendency to keep the general design of its products fairly static, with only occasional overhauls every couple of generations. For the iPhone 18e, it seems that will be the approach Apple will take once again.

In a post to Weibo early on November 3, serial leaker Fixed Focus Digital claims the iPhone 18e will be a continuation of the current design movement. It will share some of the manufacturing processes with the iPhone 18, but it won't feature many groundbreaking updates.

In the same post, the leaker adds that for the iPhone 17e, while rumors spread about it gaining the Dynamic Island at the top of the screen, they insisted that it did not. The iPhone 17e continues to use a notch.

The inclusion of that in the post may be considered a further hint about the iPhone 18e. It will probably hold on to the notch for one more generation at least.

Probable, but heard before

Weibo leakers tend to be less credible than other sources, in part due to regurgitating rumors from elsewhere. Among Weibo leakers, Fixed Focus Digital has a mixed track record.

That said, what is posted by Fixed Focus Digital sounds right, and is likely just an educated guess. It also helps that another more credible leaker posted more detail one week prior.

On October 27, another Weibo leaker gave more concrete specifications for the iPhone 18e, though again being quite similar to the iPhone 17e. That included the use of the same 6.12-inch 60Hz LTPS OLED screen as its predecessors.

The rest of the specifications were similarly predictable, including the 48-megapixel rear camera and A20 processor. There was also mention of a 24-megapixel selfie camera.

Rumor Score: Likely
